goals: Define probability, conditional probability and independence
Compute the probability of "A and B" and "A or B"
why: Classifiers output probabilities, A/B tests are probability statements, and risk models price uncertainty. Misreading conditional probability is one of the most common analytics mistakes.
explain: A **probability** is a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). Think of it as a budget of 100% belief spread across everything that could happen.
**Conditional probability** P(A | B) is the probability of A **given** that B happened. It shrinks your world to the cases where B is true. P(rain | dark clouds) is much higher than P(rain).

Events are **independent** if knowing one tells you nothing about the other (two coin flips). Then P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). For "or", add and subtract the overlap: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
The **expected value** is the long-run average: multiply each outcome by its probability and add. Insurers and casinos run entirely on expected value.

formula.plain: Probability of A given B = probability of both, divided by probability of B.

example.title: Two dice: sums, "and" and "or"
steps: Two fair dice give 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes
P(at least one 6) = 1/6 + 1/6 − 1/36 = 11/36 ≈ 0.306 (add, then subtract the overlap)
example.result: Two routes give the same 11/36. "1 minus the chance of none" is often the easiest way to answer "at least one" questions.

mistakes: Confusing P(A | B) with P(B | A): P(positive test | disease) is not P(disease | positive test).
Multiplying probabilities of events that are not independent.
takeaways: Conditioning restricts attention to cases where B is true

check.q: A bet pays ₹100 with probability 0.3, else ₹0. Expected value?

practice.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
rolls = rng.integers(1, 7, size=(100_000, 2))
print(np.mean(rolls.sum(axis=1) == 7))     # ≈ 6/36  = 0.167
print(np.mean((rolls == 6).all(axis=1)))   # ≈ 1/36  = 0.028
print(np.mean((rolls == 6).any(axis=1)))   # ≈ 11/36 = 0.306
